name: The Harm Principle
statement: The only justification for using power over someone against their will is to prevent harm to others.
meaning: The harm principle is a doctrine in political philosophy articulated by John Stuart Mill in his 1859 essay On Liberty, holding that the only legitimate reason for which power can be exercised over any member of a civilized community, against their will, is to prevent harm to others. Mill called it his one very simple principle. A person's own good, whether physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant for coercing them, so individuals should be free to act as they wish so long as their actions do not harm others. In Mill's words, the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others; his own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant. The principle rests on a distinction between self-regarding conduct, which affects only the agent and over which the individual is sovereign, and other-regarding conduct, which affects others and may be subject to social control. The harm principle stands against paternalism, the coercion of people for their own good, and against legal moralism, the enforcement of morality as such. It became foundational to liberalism and to modern thinking about civil liberties and the limits of state power.
mechanism: The harm principle works by drawing a boundary around the sphere of individual liberty that society and the state may not cross except to prevent harm to others. Mill begins from the value of individual freedom and the conviction that the coercion of a person, whether by law or by social pressure, requires justification. He argues that the only justification that qualifies is the prevention of harm to other people. This yields a distinction between two kinds of conduct. Self-regarding conduct concerns matters that affect primarily the agent themselves, such as their private choices, beliefs, tastes, and ways of life; over this domain, Mill holds, the individual is sovereign, and neither the state nor society may rightfully interfere merely because others disapprove or because they think it is for the person's own good. Other-regarding conduct affects the interests of other people, and here society may legitimately regulate, restrain, or punish in order to prevent harm. The principle thus rules out two common grounds for coercion: paternalism, protecting people from harming themselves, and legal moralism, enforcing a moral or religious code that does not involve harm to others. By limiting legitimate coercion to the prevention of harm to others, the harm principle carves out a protected space for individual liberty, including freedom of thought, expression, and lifestyle.

examples.text: Mill held that power may be used over a person against their will only to prevent harm to others, not for their own good.
Over conduct affecting only oneself, Mill argued, the individual is sovereign and society may not rightfully interfere.
The principle opposes coercing people for their own good and enforcing morality where no harm to others is done.

variants.name: The offense principle

whyItMatters: The harm principle is one of the most influential ideas in liberal political philosophy, offering a clear and powerful criterion for the proper limits of state and social power over the individual. By holding that people may be coerced only to prevent harm to others, and never merely for their own good or to enforce prevailing morality, Mill provided a foundational defense of individual liberty, freedom of thought and expression, and the right of people to live as they choose in matters that concern only themselves. The principle has profoundly shaped liberalism, constitutional rights, and debates about the reach of the law, and it remains central to arguments about free speech, drug policy, sexual conduct, euthanasia, and countless other cases where the question is whether the state may restrict conduct that others find distasteful but that harms no one else. Its distinction between self-regarding and other-regarding conduct gave a lasting vocabulary for these disputes.

limits: The harm principle is powerful but faces a central difficulty: the concept of harm is notoriously hard to define and delimit. Mill himself conceded that very little conduct is purely self-regarding, since almost any action can affect others in some way, so the protected self-regarding sphere is hard to bound in practice. This raises hard questions about which effects count as harms, whether merely being offended is a harm, and how to treat indirect, diffuse, or remote harms. The philosopher Joel Feinberg influentially argued that offense is analytically distinct from harm and might justify some legal limits under a separate offense principle, showing that the harm principle alone may not settle every case. There are also debates about harm to oneself versus others and about consented-to harms.
misreadings: The harm principle does not permit coercing people for their own good; Mill explicitly denies that a person's own physical or moral good is a sufficient warrant for interference. It does not straightforwardly resolve every case, since what counts as harm, and whether offense is harm, is genuinely contested, as Feinberg's work shows. And the self-regarding sphere is not sharply bounded, since Mill admitted almost no conduct affects only oneself, so treating the principle as licensing paternalism, as mechanically deciding cases, or as marking a clean line around private conduct, misreads a foundational but contested liberal principle.
origin: A doctrine articulated by John Stuart Mill in his 1859 essay On Liberty, holding that power may be exercised over a person against their will only to prevent harm to others; a foundation of liberalism and civil liberties.
